slides.title: What a $1,000 card balance really costs
slides.sub: Cards that charged interest averaged a 22.36% APR in Q3 2026.

slides.heading: How APR works
body: APR is the yearly interest rate on any balance you don't pay off. Cards charge it monthly, so 22.36% a year is about 1.86% a month.
Carry $1,000 and the first month's interest is about $18.63. Next month you pay interest on that interest too.

slides.heading: Slow payoff trap
body: Example: pay $35 a month on a $1,000 balance at 22.36%. It takes 42 months to pay off, and you pay about $441 in interest.
Pay $100 a month instead and it's gone in 12 months, with about $117 in interest.
slides.source: HFLIC calculation; assumes no new purchases

slides.heading: Pay in full, pay $0
body: Most cards have a grace period: pay your full statement balance by the due date and you generally aren't charged interest on purchases.
Pay only part of it and you lose that grace period. Interest hits the unpaid balance and new purchases too.
slides.source: CFPB, What is a grace period?

slides.takeaway: Treat a credit card like a debit card: only charge what you can pay off in full.

posts.caption:
Credit cards that charged interest averaged a 22.36% APR in the third quarter of 2026 (Federal Reserve). Here's what that means on a $1,000 balance.

22.36% a year is about 1.86% a month, so the first month costs about $18.63 in interest. Pay $35 a month and it takes 42 months to pay off, with about $441 in interest. Pay $100 a month and it's gone in 12 months, with about $117 in interest (example, no new purchases).

The way to pay $0: most cards have a grace period, so if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you generally aren't charged interest on purchases.

Data: Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit (Nov. 6, 2026); CFPB.
